summary: Friedrich Max Müller was an Indology, religious studies, and linguistics scholar. He earned his doctorate at Leipzig and studied under Hermann, Brockhaus, Bopp, Burnouf, and Wilson. He held professorships at Oxford (1854, 1868–1900) and was at Christ Church (~1851–1900).

Friedrich Müller worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Vienna, Tübingen, and Göttingen, including under Anton Boller. He served at the Austrian National Library (1861–1866) and as professor at the University of Vienna (from 1869).

Friedrich Nietzsche worked in philosophy and linguistics. He studied at the universities of Bonn and Leipzig, working under Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl. He served on the faculty at the University of Basel from 1869 to 1878.

Friedrich Otto Schrader was an Indology and philosophy scholar. He studied under Franz Kielhorn at Göttingen and Ernst Leumann at Strasbourg, among other institutions. He directed the Adyar Library (1905–1916) and served as professor at Kiel University (1921–1945; Gastprofessor 1947–1950).
Friedrich Ottomar Eduard Wilhelm held academic posts at the University of Munich (~1910–1922) and the University of Freiburg (~1922–1939).
Friedrich Ratzel studied at Heidelberg University around 1868. He held academic posts at the Technical University of Munich (~1875–1886) and the University of Leipzig (~1886–1904).

Friedrich Rosen worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig, Munich, Göttingen, Paris, and under Franz Bopp and Henry Thomas Colebrooke. He taught at Seminar für Orientalische Sprachen (1887–1890) and London.

Friedrich Rückert worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Würzburg, Heidelberg, Jena, and under Bopp and Hammer-Purgstall. He was a professor at Erlangen-Nuremberg (1826–1841) and Humboldt University of Berlin (1841–1849).

Friedrich Schlegel worked in Indology, philosophy, and linguistics, studying at Göttingen and Leipzig, and under Heyne, Hamilton, and Chézy. He held teaching posts at Jena (1800), Cologne (1804), and TU Dresden (1828).

Friedrich Schleiermacher worked in philosophy and religious studies. He studied at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1787–1790), where he later held a post (~1804–1807), before holding a chair at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1810–1834).

Friedrich Schrader was an Indologist and historian-archaeologist. He completed his Ph.D. under Richard Pischel at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1885–1889) and worked as a librarian at the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft (1889–1891).

Friedrich Stamm worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned his Ph.D. from the University of Münster (by 1919) and held posts at Münster's University and State Library and the Göttingen State and University Library (1921).

Friedrich Stolz was a linguist who studied at Innsbruck, Leipzig, and Graz under Bernhard Jülg and Georg Curtius. He spent his career at the University of Innsbruck as Privatdozent (1879) and professor of comparative linguistics (1886–1912).
Friedrich Streiter was an Indologist who completed his Ph.D. at Humboldt University of Berlin between 1856 and 1861, studying under Albrecht Weber in 1856.

Friedrich Weller specialized in Indology, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Leipzig under Ernst Windisch and August Conrady. He was an assistant at the Harvard-Yenching Institute (1930–1933) and held the Indian Philology chair at Leipzig (1938–1958).

Friedrich Wilhelm is an Indology and Tibetology scholar. He earned his doctorate at the University of Munich, studying under Paul Thieme. He was a professor at Munich (1969–1998) and held visiting professorships at Columbia (1965–1966) and Collège de France (1976).
Friedrich Wilhelm Graf is a scholar in religious studies and other fields. He held academic posts at the University of Augsburg (~1992–1999) and the University of Munich (~1999–2014).

Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling was a philosopher who studied at Tübingen and Leipzig. He was a professor at Jena (1798–1803), Würzburg (1803–1806), Erlangen-Nuremberg (1820–1827), Munich (1827–1841), and Berlin (1841–1845), and headed the Bavarian Academy of Sciences.

Friedrich Wilhelm Karl Müller worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Sinology, and Buddhist studies. Educated at Berlin and Leipzig under Sachau, Grube, Foy, and Gabelentz, he worked at Berlin's Ethnological Museum, serving as department director (1906–1928).

Friedrich Wilhelm Ritschl worked in linguistics and related fields. He studied at Leipzig and Halle, where he also held a post (~1829–1833). He served as professor at Breslau (1834), Bonn (1839), and Leipzig (~1865–1875).
